newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Northwest spring runoff forecast to be high.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Northwest spring runoff forecast to be high.

text.p: Spring runoff at hydroelectric projects in the Pacific Northwest will be well above average, with a few projects set to see water levels almost double the average rates, the Northwest River Forecast Center in Portland said late Friday in its February forecast.

Runoff for January to July on the Columbia River at The Dalles dam in Oregon is forecast to reach 137 percent of average, up sharply from the January forecast of 130 percent, but unchanged from the February "early bird" assessment.
Last year, runoff at The Dalles totaled 132 percent of average levels, or 139.3 million acre feet (maf) for the January-July period.
The forecast for January-July 1997 at The Dalles now stands at 145 maf, while the April-September forecast is 133 maf, or 134 percent of average.
The Dalles, the second-to-last hydroelectric project on the Columbia, is generally used as the benchmark for regional runoff due to its location and long historical record.
Other hydroelectric projects will also see well above average runoff this year, according to the center.
In-flows to Brownlee reservoir on the Snake River in Idaho are expected to reach 190 percent of average during April-July, according to the February forecast.
Also on the Snake, the Lower Granite reservoir in Washington is forecast to have in-flow of 491 maf during January-July, or 165 percent of average, the center said.

The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, which regulates reservoir levels at Northwest hydroelectric projects, is requiring extra water releases to clear space for heavy spring runoff, which could threaten some areas with flooding.
